To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the mosquito IRP1 is a bifunctional protein with iron regulatory and aconitase activities, (ii) IRP1 mRNA levels remain constant during the mosquito life cycle and after immune induction, but IRP1 binding to the IRE increases following immune induction, and (iii) the IRP1/ IRE binding activity is not regulated by changes in gene transcription but by posttranslational modification of IRP1.
IRPs are conserved in mosquitoes and that IRP binding activity can be altered during the immune response.
IRP1 proteins from the mosquitoes, A. aegpyti and A. gambia, have the same functional properties as IRP1 from other species.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of iron in the mosquito immune response to bacterial and parasitic infection.
the molecular characterization and regulation of mosquito IRPs.
the molecular basis of iron metabolism and regulation in mosquitoes, which may be useful in the development of novel insecticides and in the understanding of iron metabolism in mammals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
IRPs are conserved in the mosquito, that they bind to IREs, and that IRP/IRE interactions can change during infection.
the mosquito IRP1 protein is involved in the regulation of ferritin synthesis, but not in the regulation of succinate dehydroganase subunit b synthesis.
IRP1/IRP2 is a highly conserved gene that is regulated at the posttranslational level.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the mosquito IRPs are conserved and are not transcriptionally regulated.
the mosquito IRP1 protein is conserved, but its binding activity is not.
IRP1/ IRE binding activity is not altered in response to changes in iron, developmental stage, or infection, but is altered in response to immune induction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mosquito IRPs are similar to the mammalian IRPs, but that they are not regulated in the same way as their mammalian counterparts.
IRP1 is an immune-responsive protein in insects.
IRP1 is a key regulator of iron homeostasis in mosquitoes, but the mechanism of regulation differs in mosquitoes and humans.
